title: Triggers, Row Images and Transactional Failures
description: Trace BEFORE and AFTER row events, OLD and NEW values, multirow writes and rollback, while keeping trigger validation, audit limits and hidden side effects explicit.

questions.question_text: What activates the shown MySQL trigger?
questions.explanation: The trigger is associated with a specific event and table.

questions.question_text: When can the shown BEFORE INSERT trigger change the incoming label?
options: Before the row operation completes through an allowed NEW assignment
questions.explanation: BEFORE timing can support a defined incoming-row transformation.

questions.question_text: Which image is available for INSERT?
questions.explanation: There is no prior row image for that inserted row.

questions.question_text: Which images are available for UPDATE?
questions.explanation: The event has before and proposed/after values under its timing semantics.

questions.question_text: Which image is available for DELETE?
questions.explanation: Deletion refers to the existing row being removed.

questions.question_text: Does AFTER mean independently committed?
questions.explanation: Trigger work can remain in the surrounding transaction.

questions.question_text: How many per-row invocations can a two-row UPDATE cause?
questions.explanation: MySQL row-trigger behavior follows each affected row event.

questions.question_text: Does TRIM necessarily collapse internal spaces?
questions.explanation: The transformation removes specified edge characters, not arbitrary internal content.

questions.question_text: What happens to NULL through the shown TRIM assignment?
options: It remains NULL unless another rule changes it
questions.explanation: The function does not supply a nonnull fallback automatically.

questions.question_text: Does normalizing a blank label automatically reject it?
options: Yes, TRIM always raises an error
Only if the table is empty
questions.explanation: Rejection needs its own declared rule.

questions.question_text: Can a trigger error affect the triggering statement?
questions.explanation: Error semantics must be tested with the actual transactional participants.

questions.question_text: Does a trigger statement error prove every earlier statement in the transaction was undone?
questions.explanation: Statement scope and complete transaction scope are distinct.

questions.question_text: What should be verified for atomic update-and-log rollback?
options: Both participants use compatible transactional behavior
questions.explanation: Nontransactional effects can survive rollback.

questions.question_text: Does one tested UPDATE establish trigger coverage for every cascade orTRUNCATE path?
options: Yes, all writes activate identical triggers
questions.explanation: Different write mechanisms have engine-specific interactions.

questions.question_text: Is a row-change table automatically tamper-resistant audit evidence?
options: Only if its name is audit
questions.explanation: Privileges, coverage, identity and integrity need separate controls.

questions.question_text: What should not be copied into audit rows unnecessarily?
questions.explanation: Logging can create another sensitive data store.

questions.question_text: Can a trigger body freely modify its invoking statement’s table in every context?
options: Only if it is named recursive
Only if there is no primary key
questions.explanation: Mutating-table and stored-program restrictions must be inspected.

questions.question_text: Does a read-only query benchmark measure bulk trigger write cost?
questions.explanation: The benchmark must exercise the actual write path.

questions.question_text: What should a two-item change log contain?
options: One shared pair for every item
One old/new pair for each affected item
questions.explanation: Row images belong to individual row events.

questions.question_text: What does a syntax example alone fail to establish?
options: That the author intended a transformation
That the text names a table
Actual engine/provider execution and denied-access behavior
questions.explanation: Operational evidence must come from the actual controlled execution.

coding_problems.title: Normalize inserted item labels
coding_problems.task: Create BEFORE INSERT trigger trim_item_label on trigger_items. Assign NEW.label=TRIM(NEW.label). Insert the staged rows into trigger_items using INSERT SELECT, then return item_id and label ordered by item_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE trigger_items(item_id INT PRIMARY KEY,label VARCHAR(40) NULL) ENGINE=InnoDB; CREATE TABLE staged_items(item_id INT PRIMARY KEY,label VARCHAR(40) NULL) ENGINE=InnoDB;
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO staged_items VALUES(1,' Camera '),(2,'Desk lamp'),(3,NULL);
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE TRIGGER trim_item_label BEFORE INSERT ON trigger_items FOR EACH ROW SET NEW.label=TRIM(NEW.label); INSERT INTO trigger_items SELECT item_id,label FROM staged_items; SELECT item_id,label FROM trigger_items ORDER BY item_id;
coding_problems.expected:
item_id	label
1	Camera
2	Desk lamp
3	NULL
hints: Create the trigger before the actual insert.
coding_problems.explanation: Each inserted row is normalized through NEW; NULL and internal spaces remain as specified.

coding_problems.title: Record each quantity transition
coding_problems.task: Create AFTER UPDATE trigger quantity_change_log. Insert NEW.item_id, OLD.quantity and NEW.quantity into item_changes for each updated row. Add two to every inventory quantity, then return item_id, old_quantity, new_quantity from item_changes ordered by item_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE inventory(item_id INT PRIMARY KEY,quantity INT NOT NULL) ENGINE=InnoDB; CREATE TABLE item_changes(item_id INT NOT NULL,old_quantity INT NOT NULL,new_quantity INT NOT NULL) ENGINE=InnoDB;
coding_problems.solution_sql: CREATE TRIGGER quantity_change_log AFTER UPDATE ON inventory FOR EACH ROW INSERT INTO item_changes(item_id,old_quantity,new_quantity) VALUES(NEW.item_id,OLD.quantity,NEW.quantity); UPDATE inventory SET quantity=quantity+2; SELECT item_id,old_quantity,new_quantity FROM item_changes ORDER BY item_id;
edge_cases: A multirow update creates a record per item.
hints: Use OLD and NEW from each updated row.
coding_problems.explanation: Each affected row contributes its own old/new transition. AFTER timing does not independently commit the log.

notes:
## React to a table event without hiding the operation's contract

A trigger is a stored program activated by a specified event on its associated table. In MySQL, common trigger events are INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, with BEFORE or AFTER timing and per-row execution. The trigger can enforce a narrow transformation or record a related fact when that row event occurs. It does not replace application authorization or make every side effect safe merely because callers did not write it explicitly in their SQL.

Imagine a workshop inventory table whose labels should have no leading or trailing spaces. A BEFORE INSERT trigger can normalize the incoming label consistently for supported insert paths. A separate quantity-change log can record old and new quantities after updates. These examples have different purposes: one modifies the proposed row, the other records a change. Name those purposes and inspect their caller-visible effects before introducing either mechanism.

## Read BEFORE and AFTER as timing contracts

A BEFORE trigger runs before the row operation completes and can inspect appropriate row images. In a suitable MySQL BEFORE trigger, SET NEW.column can assign an allowed new value. An AFTER trigger runs after the row event has occurred, but remains part of the surrounding statement and transaction behavior. AFTER does not mean independently committed or guaranteed to survive a later rollback.

```sql
CREATE TRIGGER trim_item_label
BEFORE INSERT ON trigger_items
FOR EACH ROW
SET NEW.label=TRIM(NEW.label);
```

For a label containing spaces around Camera, the stored label becomes Camera under this transformation. TRIM removes the supported leading and trailing characters according to its syntax; it does not collapse every internal whitespace sequence. A NULL input remains NULL unless another rule handles it. Normalizing text must follow the domain contract rather than silently erasing meaningful characters or turning an invalid identifier into another person's identity.

## Distinguish OLD and NEW row images

INSERT supplies NEW values because no previous row exists. DELETE supplies OLD values because there is no inserted replacement row. UPDATE exposes both OLD and NEW. These names refer to the trigger event's row images, not to separate historical tables that can be joined arbitrarily. OLD values are observations rather than writable replacement fields.

For a quantity changing from five to eight, an AFTER UPDATE trigger can insert item_id, old_quantity and new_quantity into a separate change table. Another row updated in the same statement has its own images and trigger invocation. A multirow UPDATE is therefore not represented by one shared OLD/NEW pair. Predict the effect per affected row and then evaluate the whole statement's transactional outcome.

| Event | Available images | Typical example |
|---|---|---|
| INSERT | NEW | Normalize an incoming label |
| UPDATE | OLD and NEW | Record a quantity transition |
| DELETE | OLD | Record which existing identity was removed |

## Test multirow DML rather than only one example

A MySQL row trigger can execute once for every row processed by its triggering event. Updating two items can create two log rows. The trigger body must therefore be correct for each row, and its total work can scale with the affected population. A bulk import that appears to be one client statement can still invoke substantial trigger work. Measure that workload instead of assuming one statement means one trigger call.

Do not depend on an unspecified physical row-processing order for business meaning. If a log uses an increasing identifier, it can distinguish inserted log records, but a report should use an explicit ORDER BY and the required stable item identity. A business sequence requiring one specific item before another needs an explicit operation design, not an assumption about how a general multirow UPDATE scans an index.

## Understand failure and rollback scope

A trigger error can reject its triggering statement. For transactional tables, the statement's supported changes, including appropriate trigger work, participate in rollback according to the engine's documented semantics. Nontransactional participants can leave effects that cannot be reversed equivalently. Build all fixture tables before the transaction and verify their engines rather than describing every combination as atomic automatically.

An error in a later statement does not universally undo every earlier statement in an open transaction. The caller still owns the complete business operation's commit or rollback decision. A quantity-update log written by an AFTER trigger remains pending in the same transaction; rolling back the supported update can also remove that pending log. It should not be sold as an independent permanent record of every attempted action.

## Use validation and SIGNAL with explicit scope

A trigger can reject a business condition with a supported SIGNAL statement inside an appropriate compound body. For example, a rule could reject a blank normalized label. A declarative CHECK or NOT NULL constraint can be clearer for a simple row condition when the engine supports it. Choose the simplest trusted enforcement that expresses the requirement rather than moving every validation into hidden procedural code.

A compound trigger can need BEGIN/END and client-specific delimiter handling during creation. DELIMITER is a supporting client's directive, not a server SQL statement. Test the creation context and the accepted/rejected rows in a disposable lab. A syntax example in prose is not evidence that the trigger has run on a hosted judge or that production grants permit creating it.

## Recognize recursion and mutating-table restrictions

MySQL restricts operations that modify a table already being used by the statement that invoked a stored function or trigger. Triggers also have limitations on transaction control, dynamic SQL and result-set behavior. A trigger is not a general background worker that can safely call arbitrary actions during every row update. Inspect the exact server restrictions before transplanting a routine body into a trigger.

Cascading foreign-key actions have engine-specific trigger interactions; do not assume an application DELETE, a referential cascade and a TRUNCATE all activate the same row triggers. Test each relevant write path directly. A coverage claim based on one manually issued UPDATE can miss bulk loads, administrative operations or other forms of data change the system actually permits.

## Treat trigger-based auditing as limited evidence

A row-change table can help reconstruct supported data transitions, but it is not automatically a complete tamper-resistant audit system. Privileged actors can have capabilities outside ordinary application paths. Trigger definitions, log-table permissions, retention and backup protection require review. The actor identity a trigger records also needs careful interpretation under definer and connection context; it is not automatically the authenticated end user behind an application pool.

Do not log raw credentials, private request payloads or unnecessary personal data merely because a trigger can see them. A correlation reference can connect a trusted application action to a database change without copying every input. Attempted denied operations, external service calls and read access can require separate audit mechanisms. State which events the row trigger records and which remain unobserved.

## Make hidden side effects discoverable to maintainers

An UPDATE statement can look simple while triggers insert additional rows or perform validations. Document those dependencies where developers inspect the table's write contract. Include trigger definitions in reviewed schema history, inspect direct callers and plan rollback before real deployment. This lesson authors examples only and does not install a trigger in the shared application database.

Performance testing should include writes with triggers active, representative affected-row counts and failures after work begins. A read-only benchmark says little about trigger maintenance cost. Likewise, a passing arithmetic SELECT cannot prove that a trigger fired, that a transaction rollback removed its log or that a forbidden actor was denied. Match the evidence to the specific mechanism being claimed.

## Solve two row-event exercises

First exercise: create the label-normalization trigger and insert labels with surrounding spaces, a NULL and an internal space. The solutions preserve NULL and internal separation while trimming the stated outer spaces. Add an empty input table and explain why trigger creation alone does not create any item rows. If blank labels are forbidden, describe the additional declarative or signaled rule rather than pretending TRIM rejects them automatically.

Second exercise: create an AFTER UPDATE quantity-change trigger, update two synthetic items, and inspect log rows ordered by item_id. Each affected item should have its own old/new pair. Repeat inside a transaction followed by rollback and verify the supported data and log return to their prior state. Continue with [constraints](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/business-constraints), [atomicity](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/atomicity) and [database security](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/database-security-boundaries) to connect trigger behavior with broader enforcement and audit requirements.
